ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for El Paso, TX refinery piping, terminals, rail and bridge steel, plants and fab shops. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in El Paso, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection for owners in El Paso: refinery and terminal piping, storage tanks, boilers and process vessels, plant utilities and fabricated steel. Technicians travel to your site with calibrated flaw detectors, dual-element probes and step blocks, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a UT inspection quote for your El Paso site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in El Paso

El Paso is a border city where heavy industry, rail and cross-border manufacturing meet. A refinery stands a few miles east of downtown, processing crude into gasoline, distillates and other products that leave by truck, rail and pipeline. Around it sit product terminals and tank farms. The city is also a rail and trucking gateway, with the Union Pacific intermodal terminal at Santa Teresa, just across the state line in New Mexico, drawing steel-intensive logistics activity into the region. On the Mexican side, Ciudad Juárez manufacturing plants rely on utilities, boilers and process equipment that need the same inspection discipline.

That mix produces a distinctive ultrasonic workload:

  • Thickness surveys on refinery and terminal piping, heat exchanger shells and vessel walls, where sour crude, water and heat thin carbon steel unevenly.
  • Storage tank shell courses and bottom-edge areas on product and crude tanks.
  • Boiler, steam and condensate piping in manufacturing, hospital and institutional plants.
  • Groove welds on new and repaired piping and structural steel for plant projects and fabricators serving the border region.
  • Thickness checks on bridge and overpass steel plates, rail-served equipment and heavy lifting structures.

Each of these needs a trustworthy measurement of remaining steel, delivered in a form the owner's inspection group can act on.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing launches a sound pulse into metal and times the echoes that return. On a corroded wall the echo from the far surface gives remaining thickness directly. On a weld, echoes from interior features such as lack of fusion, cracks and slag reveal flaws that cannot be seen from outside. Because sound passes through carbon steel, stainless steel, aluminum and many alloys, the method is not limited by magnetic properties, and it needs access to just one surface.

Its blind spots are real, and they shape how we plan. A thickness probe reports metal under its own face, so isolated pitting between measuring points can slip through; the grid pattern and a visible A-scan reduce that risk but do not remove it. Rough, scaled or flaking surfaces scatter sound until they are cleaned. Cast components and some stainless welds have coarse grain that attenuates the beam. Very thin wall may sit below the resolution of a standard probe. We state in every report which areas were reached and which were not, because an unexamined area should never be mistaken for a clean one.

Codes and the state regime in El Paso

For in-service equipment, owners typically follow API 510 for pressure vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for aboveground storage tanks. The owner's own authorized inspector makes the fitness and remaining-life decisions; Atlantis performs the examination and reports the data, including thickness at condition monitoring locations. Contact thickness measurement is usually done in line with ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 5, with Article 23 carrying SE-797. Weld examination follows ASME Section V Article 4 for technique, while acceptance comes from the construction code, such as Appendix 12 of ASME Section VIII Division 1 or ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, or AWS D1.1 for structural groove welds.

Texas adds its own layer. Boilers and many pressure vessels fall under the state boiler law administered by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, which runs a boiler program with its own inspection requirements. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code. Intrastate pipelines are overseen by the Railroad Commission of Texas under rules that incorporate the federal standards in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195. Refining and chemical sites also fall under the process safety management rule in OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119. For a plain-language view of technique rules, see our guide to ASME Section V Article 5.

How the ultrasonic work is performed

A thickness job starts with calibration on a step block made of the same alloy as the part. On corroded or pitted metal a dual-element probe is preferred, since its separate transmitting and receiving crystals handle rough back surfaces better. The technician watches the A-scan trace on screen, so a double echo or a lamination is recognized instead of being recorded as a valid number. Hot piping near a refinery or boiler house calls for high-temperature probes and couplant, and readings are corrected for temperature if the procedure requires it. Every reading is mapped to a numbered point on a grid or isometric sketch, so the next survey can return to exactly the same spot.

Weld inspection uses an angle-beam probe, generally 45, 60 or 70 degrees, to send shear waves through the joint. A reference level is set from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, the weld and adjacent base metal are scanned from both sides where geometry permits, and any signal above the recording level is evaluated for location, length and amplitude. The Level II doing the work interprets the signals against the code's table on the spot.

Turning readings into decisions

A single set of thickness numbers answers one question: how much wall exists now. Two sets answer a better one: how fast is it going. Dividing the loss between surveys by the time between them gives a corrosion rate, and dividing the remaining margin by that rate gives remaining life, which is what sets the next inspection date or a replacement budget. For this to work the readings must be repeatable, so we keep consistent point numbering, retain raw data and record the probe, calibration block and temperature each time. Any location reading below minimum required thickness, or changing faster than the earlier trend, is flagged at the top of the report so your inspector sees it before anything else.

UT on boilers, steam and utility systems

Plants across El Paso and the border region depend on steam. Boilers, economizers, deaerators and condensate return lines thin through erosion, flow-accelerated corrosion and under-deposit attack, and ultrasonic thickness readings are the standard way to watch it happen. Elbows and tees downstream of control valves, desuperheaters and steam traps are the usual hot spots, because turbulence strips the protective oxide from the pipe wall. A survey normally lays out readings around the circumference of each fitting and a few feet upstream and downstream, on a spacing the procedure states. Where insulation hides the pipe, the owner removes small windows at agreed locations so the crew can reach bare metal, and the windows are restored afterward. For boilers regulated by the state, a thickness report supports the data the commissioned inspector reviews at the next statutory inspection. Weld examinations are also common here when tubes, headers or attachment welds are replaced and the code calls for volumetric examination of the repair.

Who does the work

Technicians who perform and interpret UT are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and evaluates results; an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Procedures are approved by Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT NDT Level III with credentials in all five conventional methods used here. Procedures are written against the code edition in your contract. If your own written practice needs development or review, see our written practice development and Level III consulting pages.

What the report contains

Reports identify the component and its location, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe, calibration block and couplant, the surface temperature, the technician and level, and the date. Thickness surveys come with a grid or sketch showing each reading beside nominal and minimum wall, with out-of-tolerance points marked. Weld examinations list each recordable indication with position, length and amplitude, and a clear accept or reject call against the named criteria. Raw data is preserved so later surveys can be compared point by point, and anything that could not be examined is listed along with the reason.

Planning a UT job in El Paso

El Paso's high desert climate sets the practical limits. Summer sun can drive dark steel surfaces far above the temperature range of ordinary probes and couplants, so high-temperature materials are written into the scope and work is planned for cooler parts of the day. Winter nights are cold enough to thicken couplant at times, though days are mild. Fine dust is constant and gets into gear, so probes and calibration blocks are kept clean. Refineries and terminals require safety orientation, badging and permits, and border-region plants may have their own access rules, so we ask for site requirements early and send technician names and qualification records ahead. Atlantis has no office in El Paso, so crews travel to your site, and we plan travel, lodging and scope together, aligning with your outage calendar. The Texas inspection services page provides additional statewide context.

Choosing UT, MT or PT in El Paso

Pick ultrasonic testing when you need remaining wall or want to know whether a weld is sound through its thickness. Pick magnetic particle inspection in El Paso for surface cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel, such as weld toes and lifting lugs. Pick liquid penetrant testing in El Paso for surface-breaking flaws on stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys. Many jobs combine methods, with thickness first and surface checks on repaired areas afterward. Our national ultrasonic testing page explains the method more broadly.

Training your own technicians in El Paso

Plants and shops with steady inspection needs often qualify their own staff. Our UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 programs are built around SNT-TC-1A, with practice in the UT simulator, and the El Paso training page explains how courses and employer-run practicals fit together. The employer, not the instructor, issues the certification under SNT-TC-1A, so we build the training and records your program needs.

faq.q: Can you perform ultrasonic thickness testing on El Paso refinery piping?
faq.a: Yes, within the scope your site allows. Technicians travel to the facility, follow your safety and permit rules, take readings at the locations you specify, and deliver a report your inspection group uses for corrosion rates.

faq.q: Where do your El Paso technicians travel from?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in El Paso. No. Atlantis has no office in El Paso, so crews travel to the site for the scope you agree. Everyone on the job is qualified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A under our written practice, and access is planned before mobilization.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness while equipment is running?
faq.a: Often yes. Contact thickness readings are taken from the outside, so equipment can stay in service if the surface is accessible, safe to approach and within the probe's temperature limit. Hot surfaces need high-temperature probes and couplant.

faq.q: What is the difference between UT and magnetic particle or penetrant testing?
faq.a: UT measures remaining wall and finds flaws inside welds. Magnetic particle and penetrant testing find only flaws that reach the surface. The right choice depends on whether your concern is thinning, weld quality or surface cracking.

faq.q: Which standards do El Paso UT reports follow?
faq.a: Reports cite the documents on your order, usually ASME Section V for technique, ASTM E797 for thickness, and a construction code such as ASME Section VIII, ASME B31.3 or AWS D1.1 for acceptance. Fitness decisions stay with your inspector.

faq.q: Do you replace our API authorized inspector?
faq.a: No. Your authorized inspector signs for the equipment under API 510, 570 or 653. Atlantis supplies the ultrasonic readings and a report that feeds your inspector's remaining-life calculations.

faq.q: How should surfaces be prepared for ultrasonic thickness testing?
faq.a: Remove loose scale, flaking paint and heavy rust so the probe couples well. Thin, well-bonded coatings may be measured through when the procedure allows it, but rough corrosion usually needs wire brushing or grinding first.

faq.q: Can UT find every pit in a corroded wall?
faq.a: No method can promise that. A thickness probe reads only the metal beneath it, so the grid spacing in the procedure matters, and the report states which areas were reached and which were not so nothing is assumed.

faq.q: Can you train our El Paso staff in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer UT Level 1 and Level 2 training built around SNT-TC-1A, with simulator practice, and we can help write your written practice. Certification of your staff stays with your company once training and experience requirements are met.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in El Paso, TX | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing for El Paso, TX refinery welds, rail and bridge steel, cranes and fabricated steel. Request an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in El Paso, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel for El Paso owners: refinery and terminal welds, rail-served equipment, lifting gear and cranes, bridge and overpass steel, and fabricated structures. Crews travel to your site with yokes, particles and light meters, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a mag particle testing quote for your El Paso site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in El Paso

El Paso steel works under repeated load. Trains and trucks move constantly through the border gateway, interstate bridges flex under traffic, cranes and hoists lift freight and plant equipment, and a refinery east of downtown runs rotating machinery and pressure piping around the clock. Fatigue cracking begins at the surface, usually at a weld toe or an abrupt change of section, which is exactly where the magnetic method concentrates its sensitivity.

Typical MT work in the El Paso area includes:

  • Weld toes, nozzle attachments and repair excavations on refinery and terminal vessels and piping.
  • Crane runway girders, hook blocks, shackles, spreader beams and other lifting hardware at plants and freight yards.
  • Welds on rail-served equipment, trailers, chassis and loading structures near the border crossings.
  • Structural steel connections on bridges, overpasses and sign structures along the interstate corridor.
  • Fabricated steel at shops that build frames, supports and process equipment for plants on both sides of the border.

Finding a crack while it is a shallow surface indication usually means a grinding repair rather than a replacement.

What magnetic particle testing finds and what it misses

The method magnetizes the steel and dusts or sprays fine iron particles over it. A crack interrupts the flux and pushes a tiny leakage field out of the surface; particles cluster there and draw the flaw's outline in a few seconds. It is quick, portable and very sensitive to tight cracks, and it also reveals flaws just under the surface.

The limits are firm. Only ferromagnetic material can be examined, which means carbon and low-alloy steel; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not qualify. The method sees surface and near-surface flaws and says nothing about the interior of a thick weld or the remaining wall. A crack running parallel to the field produces almost no signal, which is why every area is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. Heavy coatings, scale and oil weaken the response. When a job needs wall thickness or internal weld quality, we point to ultrasonic testing instead of stretching MT past its capability.

Codes behind MT work in El Paso

Technique rules come from ASME Section V Article 7, and many owners also cite ASTM E709 as a guide and ASTM E1444 as the practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridge welding, the code that state transportation agencies use for steel bridges. Pipeline welds follow API 1104 and the federal pipeline rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, and the Railroad Commission of Texas oversees intrastate pipeline safety. Texas boilers and many pressure vessels are covered by the state boiler law that the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation administers, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. At covered refineries, the OSHA rule at 29 CFR 1910.119 requires mechanical integrity inspections. Our explanation of ASME Section V Article 7 details the technique requirements.

How the magnetic particle work is done

Most field examinations use an electromagnetic yoke. Before use the yoke is proven by lifting a test weight: at least 10 pounds for an AC yoke and at least 40 pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at the widest pole spacing used. The technician places the yoke on the weld, applies dry powder or wet suspension while the field is on, and reads the particle pattern. The area is then examined again with the yoke turned about ninety degrees so cracks in every direction are caught. Prods are used only where the code allows and arc burns can be prevented.

Contrasting visible particles work well outdoors on cleaned welds, and El Paso's strong sun can be a help or a nuisance depending on the shade available. Fluorescent particles are more sensitive but need UV-A light in a darkened enclosure. Indications are measured, classified and compared with the acceptance table, and residual magnetism is checked afterward and removed when it could disturb welding, machining or instruments.

Preparing the surface and checking the equipment

Particles cannot cling to steel through rust scale, heavy paint or oil. The procedure states how clean the weld and the surrounding band must be, and in practice wire brushing or light grinding is normal, with blasted weld areas giving the cleanest result. Sharp corners, threads and section changes create nonrelevant indications that a technician must tell apart from cracks. On the equipment side, yokes are tested for lifting power, light meters are within calibration, and wet baths are tested for particle concentration so a weak suspension does not hide a crack. If a check fails, work stops until it is corrected, and calibration records go on the report so an owner can confirm everything was in date.

Fatigue cracking in crossing, rail and crane steel

The structures that carry El Paso's cross-border freight share one trait: they see millions of load cycles. Crane runway girders and trolley rails collect small cracks at stiffener welds and flange-to-web joints. Trailer and chassis frames crack at cross-member welds and spring hangers. Bridge details such as welded cover plates and attachment plates become fatigue-prone because the weld toe is a stress raiser. When an inspector finds a crack at one of these details, the remedy usually depends on how long it is and whether it sits in primary tension steel, so the length and position recorded on the MT report matter as much as the finding itself. Where a crack is ground out, we examine the excavation until the indication is gone and the welder can proceed with a clean, documented starting point.

Who does the work

Magnetic particle technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The person on your site is a Level II who runs the examination and calls the indications, and a Level III stands behind the written procedure and the report review. Procedure approval rests with Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, for the conventional methods we offer in the United States. Procedures follow the code edition in your contract, and our Level III consulting page describes how we can help you align your own documents.

Wet or dry: choosing the technique for El Paso conditions

Dry powder is quick and convenient on rough, warm surfaces, and it is the usual choice when a weld has to be checked on a hot day without cleaning gear. Its weakness is wind. A steady desert breeze blows the powder off the steel before it can settle into a field, so dry work outdoors calls for a windbreak or a different technique. Wet suspension, carried in a spray bottle or aerosol, clings better and gives higher sensitivity on smooth, cleaned surfaces, but it dries fast under direct sun. In practice a crew carries both and decides on arrival. The procedure states which forms are allowed, the minimum field strength and the way the technician proves it, and the report records the technique actually used. Where indications are marginal, the examination is repeated with the other technique or under different lighting before a call is made, so that a decision to accept or reject does not rest on a single look.

Repair cycles and records

When a rejectable indication is found, the area is marked and the repair is agreed with the owner or fabricator. After grinding, the excavation is examined again until no indication remains, then examined once more after rewelding and any required heat treatment. The report keeps the first indication, the excavation check and the final examination together, so a reviewer can see the whole repair sequence and the condition of the steel at the end of it.

What the MT report contains

Reports name the component and area examined, the procedure and revision, the magnetizing technique, the yoke serial number and last verification, the particle type and color, the surface condition, the technician and level, and the date. Each recordable indication is described by location, orientation and length, with an accept or reject call against the named criteria and a sketch or photograph that lets a welder find the exact spot. Areas that could not be examined, for example because of access or coating, are listed so no one assumes they were covered.

Planning an MT job in El Paso

Desert weather matters. Midday sun can heat dark steel enough to dry wet particles before they work, so early or late scheduling and shade are common, and winter mornings can be cold enough to slow a suspension. Dust and wind are routine and interfere with dry powder, which is why wet methods are often chosen outdoors. Refinery and terminal sites require safety orientation and permits, border-region plants have their own access procedures, and we ask for them early and send technician names and qualification records ahead. Atlantis has no office in El Paso, so crews travel to your site; we plan travel, lodging and scope together. The Texas inspection services page gives more statewide context.

MT, PT or UT for your El Paso job

Use magnetic particle inspection for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel. Use liquid penetrant testing in El Paso for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic alloys or surfaces that cannot be magnetized. Use ultrasonic testing in El Paso when the question is remaining wall or subsurface weld quality. The national magnetic particle testing page and our MT versus PT comparison help you decide.

Training your own technicians in El Paso

Plants and shops with steady needs often qualify staff to run routine checks. Our MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 courses are built around SNT-TC-1A, and the El Paso training page explains how courses and employer practicals fit together. SNT-TC-1A leaves certification with the employer, which means we focus on the knowledge, practice hours and records behind it.

faq.q: What flaws does magnetic particle inspection find?
faq.a: It finds cracks, laps, seams and similar discontinuities that are open to the surface or just beneath it in ferromagnetic steel. It cannot find flaws deep in a weld or measure how much wall remains.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel or aluminum?
faq.a: No. Austenitic stainless steel and aluminum are not ferromagnetic, so the magnetic field the method needs cannot form. Liquid penetrant testing is the usual alternative for those materials.

faq.q: Is Atlantis located in El Paso?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in El Paso. No. Atlantis has no office in El Paso, so a crew travels to your site for the scope you agree. Each person is qualified to ASNT SNT-TC-1A under the company's written practice, and we confirm access first.

faq.q: Which standards govern magnetic particle work on El Paso bridge steel?
faq.a: Steel bridge welding generally falls under AWS D1.5, with technique from ASME Section V Article 7 or the procedure your contract names. The report cites the exact documents and edition used.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required?
faq.a: No. It is required when residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, instruments or later service. The procedure says when it applies, and the technician checks the remaining field and records the result.

faq.q: How is a yoke verified before use?
faq.a: By a lifting test. An AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds at the widest pole spacing used. The result is recorded, and a yoke that fails is taken out of use.

faq.q: Is visible or fluorescent particle better for field work?
faq.a: Visible particles suit most outdoor work on cleaned welds. Fluorescent particles detect finer flaws but need UV-A light in a darkened area, so they are used when a tent or shop can be arranged.

faq.q: Will you serve as the API authorized inspector for our refinery equipment?
faq.a: No. Responsibility for the vessel or piping stays with your authorized inspector under API 510 or 570. We run the magnetic particle examination and deliver findings in a report built for that inspector's review.

faq.q: Can you train our El Paso staff in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. We offer MT Level 1 and Level 2 training built around SNT-TC-1A and can help you write your written practice. Your company issues the certification itself after documenting the training and experience each person has completed.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in El Paso, TX | LPT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for El Paso, TX stainless piping, alloy welds, valves, boilers and fabricated parts. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in El Paso, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for El Paso owners: stainless and alloy piping welds, boiler and heat exchanger components, valve bodies, aluminum parts and repair areas that cannot be magnetized. Crews travel to your site with penetrant systems, cleaners and developers, follow a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a dye penetrant quote for your El Paso site and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in El Paso

Penetrant testing is the method of choice where steel is not magnetic or the shape defeats a magnetic field. El Paso has plenty of that work. The refinery and terminals east of downtown use stainless and alloy components in process piping, instrument connections and heat exchangers. Plants serving the border manufacturing economy run boilers, steam systems and food or pharmaceutical-grade stainless piping. Fabrication and repair shops weld aluminum, stainless and nickel alloy parts, and a penetrant check is the portable way to confirm a weld has no cracks open to the surface.

Typical PT work in the El Paso area includes:

  • Root and cover passes on stainless steel and alloy pipe welds in process and utility systems.
  • Valve bodies, weld overlays and repaired pressure-containing parts.
  • Boiler tube attachment welds, drum nozzles and heat exchanger components.
  • Aluminum trailers, tanks and frames used in freight and cross-border logistics.
  • Machined faces, threads and seal surfaces on rotating equipment and valves.

The process needs no power supply, so it travels easily to rooftops, pipe racks and remote work areas.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

A liquid penetrant is applied to a clean, dry surface and seeps into any opening that reaches the surface. After the excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so that it shows as a visible line or dot. Cracks, laps, porosity and lack of fusion at the surface are revealed on almost any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

It detects only surface-breaking discontinuities. A flaw buried inside a weld, or metal thinning from corrosion, will not be found. Anything that closes the opening defeats the test, including paint, oil, scale and metal smeared across a crack by grinding or blasting. Porous surfaces hold penetrant and produce false marks. That is why cleaning and preparation are written into the procedure, and why the report says how each surface was prepared.

Codes behind PT work in El Paso

Technique rules come from ASME Section V Article 6, and many contracts also cite ASTM E165 for industrial practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping and AWS D1.1 for structural welds. Pipeline welds follow API 1104 and the federal rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with the Railroad Commission of Texas overseeing intrastate pipeline safety. Many Texas boilers and pressure vessels are subject to the state boiler law run by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. At covered process facilities the OSHA rule at 29 CFR 1910.119 requires mechanical integrity inspections. For a closer look at the technique rules, read our guide to ASME Section V Article 6.

How the penetrant work is done

The sequence runs pre-clean, apply, dwell, remove, develop, inspect, post-clean. Oil, paint, scale and spatter are removed and the surface is allowed to dry fully, because solvent left in a crack dilutes the penetrant. Penetrant goes on by spray, brush or dip and sits for the dwell time the procedure sets for the material, temperature and expected flaw. Excess is removed with solvent wipes or a controlled water rinse, taking care not to pull penetrant from real flaws, then a thin even coat of developer is applied and given time to bleed out indications.

Visible red dye suits most field work in daylight, while fluorescent systems detect finer flaws but need darkness and UV-A light. For stainless steel and nickel alloys, materials with controlled sulfur and halogen content are used, and post-cleaning removes residue so nothing harms the metal in service. Indications are evaluated during the development window, measured, recorded and photographed.

Choosing the system and reading the indications

Solvent-removable visible systems are the usual field choice on welds because they need no water. Water-washable systems suit rougher or larger surfaces, and fluorescent systems are chosen for fine cracks in critical alloy parts. We select the system based on alloy, finish, expected flaw size, temperature and code, and record it on the report. Reading the result takes judgment: a relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity, a nonrelevant one comes from a thread root or sharp corner, and a false one comes from the process itself, such as poorly removed penetrant. The procedure sets how doubtful marks are evaluated, usually by wiping and re-developing, and every mark evaluated is documented, including those judged nonrelevant.

PT on boilers, exchangers and food-grade stainless

Many El Paso plants operate stainless systems where cleanliness matters as much as strength. Dairy, beverage, pharmaceutical and packaging lines use polished stainless piping, and a crack in a sanitary weld is both a leak path and a place for bacteria to hide. Heat exchangers and boilers use alloys where welds are checked after repair, and a small crack in a tube-to-tubesheet weld can let process fluids cross. Penetrant testing is well suited to these jobs because it is gentle, needs no electricity and leaves no magnetic field, provided the materials are selected for low halogen and sulfur content and the part is cleaned thoroughly afterward. On sanitary systems we coordinate with the plant's own cleaning and validation procedures so residues are removed completely before the line returns to service, and the report records which materials were used and how the cleanup was done.

Who does the work

Penetrant technicians are qualified under the company's written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The technician applying the materials is a Level II who interprets the result, while a Level III reviews reports and signs off the written method. Anoop Rayavarapu, an ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, approves the penetrant procedure before crews mobilize. Procedures follow the code edition in your contract, and our Level III consulting page describes support for reviewing your own penetrant procedure.

Verifying the system before and during the work

Penetrant materials can lose strength, and a system that does not work gives a false sense of security. Before an examination the technician checks that materials are in date, from the same family and from batches recorded on the report. A cracked reference panel or comparator block can be used to confirm that the system still shows fine cracks at the temperature of the day, which matters when the metal is warm from the El Paso sun. Light levels are verified for visible work, and UV-A intensity and ambient white light are verified for fluorescent work. If conditions change during a job, for example a gust of dust or a sudden temperature shift, the technician repeats the affected area rather than hoping the earlier work still stands. All of this is documented, so that an owner or auditor can see not only what was found but how confidently it could have been found.

After the test: repairs, re-examination and records

A rejected indication starts a short chain of events. The defect is marked, the repair method is agreed with the owner or fabricator, and after grinding or welding the area is cleaned and examined again with the same procedure. Penetrant bleed-out from a ground-out crack can be misleading if the metal has not been cleaned thoroughly, so the area is cleaned and dried before the re-examination begins. We keep the original indication record next to the re-examination result, so the file shows what was found, what was done and what the surface looked like when the repair was accepted. For alloy and stainless parts that must stay clean for service, the final post-clean is recorded as its own step.

What the PT report contains

Reports name the component and area, the procedure and revision, the penetrant family and method, manufacturer and batch numbers for the penetrant, remover and developer, the surface preparation, part and ambient temperatures, dwell and development times, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is recorded with location, size and type, with an accept or reject call against the named criteria and a sketch or photograph. Areas that could not be examined, for example because of insulation or access, are listed, and batch numbers keep materials traceable on stainless and nickel alloys.

Planning a PT job in El Paso

Temperature rules penetrant work. ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard range of about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials, and the procedure must be qualified for any other temperature. El Paso summers can drive dark metal past the upper limit by midday, and winter mornings sometimes dip below the lower one, so we plan early or late scheduling, shade or warming. Wind carries dust onto wet surfaces and developer, and sheltering the work area helps. Refinery and terminal sites require safety orientation and permits, and border-region plants have their own access procedures, so we ask early and send technician names and qualification records ahead. faq.q: What does penetrant testing detect?
faq.a: Liquid penetrant testing detects cracks, laps, porosity and lack of fusion that are open to the surface of a non-porous material. It does not find flaws sealed under the surface or measure corrosion loss.

faq.q: Can you penetrant-test stainless steel and aluminum in El Paso?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant works on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and other non-magnetic metals that magnetic particle inspection cannot examine. Low sulfur and halogen materials are specified for stainless and nickel alloys.

faq.q: How does El Paso weather affect penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard temperature range is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Summer sun can push dark steel above it and winter mornings can fall below it, so we plan timing, shade or warming, or use a procedure qualified for the actual temperature.

faq.q: Why does PT need such careful cleaning?
faq.a: Penetrant can enter only a clean, open flaw. Paint, scale, oil and metal smeared by grinding can seal a crack and hide it, so cleaning is part of the procedure and the report records how the surface was prepared.

faq.q: What is the difference between a relevant and a nonrelevant indication?
faq.a: A relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity and is measured against acceptance criteria. A nonrelevant one comes from a feature such as a thread root or sharp corner. Both are documented so the reasoning is visible.

faq.q: Visible dye or fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye is viewed in white light and suits most field work. Fluorescent penetrant detects finer indications but needs darkness and UV-A light, so we use it where a tent, shed or shop can be arranged.

faq.q: Do you act as the API authorized inspector at our facility?
faq.a: No. Under the API codes the person who signs for the equipment is your own authorized inspector. We perform the penetrant examination and provide a report written for that inspector's use.
